story_text: In my typical day in 2050 I wake up early on Sunday and walk to the shared oven at the end of our street. Every building has a slot, and today is ours. I bring the dough I left rising overnight and talk with the neighbours while it bakes. Most weekdays I eat quick meals from the canteen at work, but Sunday is different. We bring the bread home, open a tin of sardines, slice tomatoes from the balcony and eat slowly with my flatmates. It feels like the oldest thing we still do, and I like that.
title: Sunday Bread, Shared Ovens
swipe_hook: The neighbourhood oven still smells like my grandmother's kitchen.
image_prompt: Neighbours holding bowls of dough outside a shared brick oven on a narrow street, morning light.
bio: The neighbourhood oven still smells like my grandmother's kitchen.
summary: A young woman in Portugal bakes bread in a shared neighbourhood oven every Sunday and eats it slowly with her flatmates. Weekdays are rushed canteen meals, which makes the Sunday ritual feel precious.

story_text: In 2050 my kitchen has a food printer that makes fresh pasta in any shape in two minutes. It is useful when I come home late from the lab. The flour cartridges are made from insects and lentils, so it is cheap and healthy, and the app counts the protein for me. Still, on Fridays I switch it off and make tagliatelle by hand like my father taught me, because it is the only time I really cook. My friends say I am being romantic. Maybe, but the printed pasta never tastes like anything I remember.
title: Pasta Printed to Order
swipe_hook: The printer makes perfect pasta, but I still knead it myself on Fridays.
image_prompt: A compact food printer extruding fresh pasta next to a wooden board dusted with flour.
bio: The printer makes perfect pasta, but I still knead it myself on Fridays.
summary: An Italian man uses a food printer for quick protein-rich pasta on weekdays but makes it by hand on Fridays as his father taught him. He finds the printed version practical yet tasteless.

story_text: In my day in 2050 I finish work at four, because most of us work shorter weeks now. I go up to the rooftop garden of our building, where we grow tomatoes, beans, peppers and even a small rice tray in water boxes. Tonight it is my turn to cook for the whole floor, so I make a big paella with what we picked and a little chicken from the cooperative. Fourteen people eat together at long tables. Food costs more than before, but sharing it makes it cheaper and much more fun.
title: Rooftop Paella, City Rice
swipe_hook: Half of tonight's paella grew on our own roof.
image_prompt: A large paella pan on a rooftop garden at sunset, long tables and planter boxes around it.
bio: Half of tonight's paella grew on our own roof.
summary: A Spanish woman with a shorter working week cooks paella for her whole building floor using vegetables and rice grown on their rooftop. Shared cooking keeps expensive food affordable and sociable.

story_text: My day in 2050 starts with a message from my nutrition app telling me what I need to eat today based on my sleep and my blood sugar. Breakfast is a green shake, lunch is a bowl delivered to the office, all calculated. It works, I have more energy than my parents had at my age. But in the evening I buy a small piece of real cheese from the market and eat it with bread, and the app shows a little red warning. I accept the warning. Some things are not data.
title: Nutrition Plan, Cheese Exception
swipe_hook: My health app plans every meal, except the cheese I refuse to give up.
image_prompt: A phone showing a meal plan beside a small piece of cheese and a slice of bread on a market paper.
bio: My health app plans every meal, except the cheese I refuse to give up.
summary: A Frenchman follows a nutrition app that plans meals from his health data and feels more energetic, but keeps eating real cheese in the evening despite the app's warnings.

story_text: In 2050 meat from animals is rare and expensive, so most of what we eat is cultivated or plant based. On Saturdays I go to the weekly market with my son and we buy vegetables, potatoes and a box of cultivated pork for schnitzel. It tastes almost the same as the one my mother made. We cook together and he breads the slices with too much flour, which is my favourite part. I do not miss the old way much. The food changed, but the kitchen did not.
title: Cultivated Meat, Weekly Market
swipe_hook: The schnitzel is grown in a tank now, and nobody at the table minds.
image_prompt: A mother and son breading schnitzel at a kitchen counter, vegetables from the market in a basket.
bio: The schnitzel is grown in a tank now, and nobody at the table minds.
summary: A German mother buys cultivated meat and market vegetables on Saturdays and cooks schnitzel with her son. She accepts the shift away from animal meat because the shared kitchen routine stayed the same.

story_text: In my day in 2050 the weather decides what we eat. After another wet summer half the harvest is gone, so food comes in a weekly box from the council. Potatoes, oats, some frozen fish if we are lucky. I cook soup for my sister and me on a small induction plate because energy is limited in the evening. Restaurants are for rich people now. I try not to think about it too much, but every year the box gets smaller and the queue gets longer.
title: Rations, Rain and Potatoes
swipe_hook: We queue for the weekly box and hope the potatoes survived the floods.
image_prompt: A long queue in the rain outside a council building, people holding cardboard food boxes.
bio: We queue for the weekly box and hope the potatoes survived the floods.
summary: A young Irishman lives on weekly council food boxes after floods destroy harvests, cooking soup on limited energy for himself and his sister. He feels the boxes shrinking and the queues growing.

story_text: In 2050 our flat has a cooking robot that prepares dinner while I am still on the train home. It follows recipes from my grandmother's notebook that I scanned years ago, so the curry tastes like hers. I come home, the table is set, and my partner and I eat together without stress. The robot does not do desserts well, so on weekends I bake a crumble with apples from the community orchard. It is small, but it makes the evening feel like ours.
title: Robot Chef, Human Dessert
swipe_hook: The robot cooks dinner, but dessert is still my job.
image_prompt: A kitchen robot arm stirring a pot of curry while a young woman takes an apple crumble out of the oven.
bio: The robot cooks dinner, but dessert is still my job.
summary: A British woman relies on a cooking robot programmed with her grandmother's recipes for weeknight dinners, and keeps baking desserts herself at the weekend with apples from a community orchard.

story_text: In 2050 I live alone in a small apartment in Copenhagen and work from home most days. Lunch is rye bread with smoked fish and vegetables from a subscription box. For dinner I usually cook a simple stew in one pot while listening to the radio. Once a week there is a dinner club in the building where everyone brings something. Eating alone does not bother me. I think food in 2050 is less about big families and more about small habits you can keep.
title: Eating Alone, Eating Well
swipe_hook: I eat alone most nights, and the food is good enough to make it fine.
image_prompt: A small apartment table with one bowl of stew, rye bread and a radio by the window at dusk.
bio: I eat alone most nights, and the food is good enough to make it fine.
summary: A Danish man living alone cooks simple one-pot dinners and joins a weekly dinner club in his building. He sees food in 2050 as small sustainable habits rather than big family meals.

story_text: In 2050 I have lived in Porto for twenty years, but I still cook like my mother in São Paulo on special days. Today is my daughter's birthday, so I spend the morning making feijoada with black beans, smoked tofu instead of so much pork, and Portuguese kale from the market. My neighbours bring pastéis de nata. The kitchen is loud and full of two languages. Every year the recipe changes a little, and I think that is how traditions survive.
title: Two Kitchens, One Feijoada
swipe_hook: My feijoada is half Brazilian, half Portuguese, and fully mine.
image_prompt: A crowded kitchen with a big pot of black beans, kale on the counter and a birthday table behind.
bio: My feijoada is half Brazilian, half Portuguese, and fully mine.
summary: A Brazilian woman in Porto cooks a hybrid feijoada for her daughter's birthday, mixing Brazilian beans with Portuguese kale and less meat, while neighbours bring pastries.

story_text: In 2050 most vegetables in Milan come from vertical farms inside old office buildings. They are clean and cheap, but my family kept my grandmother's garden outside the city. Every weekend I take the train there and work the soil with my cousins. We grow tomatoes, zucchini and basil, and we make sauce together in August. People think it is inefficient. For us it is a way of saying that food is not only a product.
title: Grandmother's Garden Stays
swipe_hook: They offered us vertical farm vegetables, we kept the old garden instead.
image_prompt: Cousins picking tomatoes in a sunny garden with the city skyline far away.
bio: They offered us vertical farm vegetables, we kept the old garden instead.
summary: An Italian woman and her cousins keep tending their grandmother's garden outside Milan instead of relying on vertical farms, making tomato sauce together each August.

story_text: In my day in 2050 the water allowance in Valencia is strict, and the app shows the water cost of every meal before I cook. Rice became expensive after the long droughts, so paella is only for celebrations. Most days I eat chickpeas, bread and vegetables that need little water. I am not hungry, but I am always counting. Sometimes I worry about what my children will eat if the droughts keep getting worse.
title: Water Bills Decide Dinner
swipe_hook: Every recipe now starts with how much water it costs.
image_prompt: A phone screen showing the water cost of a meal next to a bowl of chickpeas in a dry, bright kitchen.
bio: Every recipe now starts with how much water it costs.
summary: A Spanish man in Valencia plans meals around a strict water allowance, reserving rice dishes for celebrations and eating mostly chickpeas and vegetables. He worries about future droughts.

story_text: In 2050 I work as a teacher, and the best part of my day is lunch. Our school canteen is also a kitchen class: every week a different group of students cooks for everyone with a chef. Today they made a lentil and vegetable gratin and a fruit tart. The kids know where every ingredient comes from and how much it costs. When I was young most people my age could not cook at all. Now it feels like cooking is coming back.
title: Canteen That Teaches Cooking
swipe_hook: Our school canteen became the place where everyone learns to cook.
image_prompt: Students in aprons serving a lentil gratin to classmates in a bright school canteen.
bio: Our school canteen became the place where everyone learns to cook.
summary: A French teacher describes a school canteen where students cook lunch for everyone with a chef each week, learning where food comes from. She sees cooking skills returning.

story_text: In 2050 I work night shifts at the hospital in Berlin. When I come home at seven in the morning, my mother has left a pot of red lentil soup in the shared fridge of our building, with a note. I heat it, add lemon and chili, and eat it by the window while the city wakes up. On my days off I cook for her in return, usually something quick like pasta with vegetables. It is a small exchange, but it keeps us close.
title: Night Shift, Warm Lentils
swipe_hook: After the night shift, my mother's lentil soup is waiting in the shared fridge.
image_prompt: A man eating lentil soup by a window at sunrise, a handwritten note on the table.
bio: After the night shift, my mother's lentil soup is waiting in the shared fridge.
summary: A man working night shifts in Berlin eats the lentil soup his mother leaves in the shared fridge, and cooks for her on his days off in return.

story_text: In 2050 seaweed farming is one of the biggest jobs on the west coast, and I work on one of the farms near Galway. We eat it in soups, breads and even desserts. For dinner I make a stew with potatoes, carrots and kelp, and fish when the quota allows. My friends from the city laugh that everything tastes like the sea. I like it. It feels local and it does not need much land or water.
title: Seaweed on Every Plate
swipe_hook: Seaweed was a curiosity; now it is in almost everything I cook.
image_prompt: Seaweed lines on a grey sea near the coast, a pot of stew with kelp on a stove inside a cottage.
bio: Seaweed was a curiosity; now it is in almost everything I cook.
summary: An Irish woman working on a seaweed farm near Galway cooks with seaweed in most dishes and sees it as a local, low-impact food.

story_text: My typical day in 2050 is efficient. Breakfast and lunch are meal pods delivered every morning, balanced for my training plan, and I barely think about food. It saves time and money. On Friday nights though, I meet friends at the pub, which now serves mostly plant-based pies and chips. We sit for hours. I sometimes feel that food during the week has become fuel, and the weekend is where it is still about people.
title: Meal Pods and Real Pubs
swipe_hook: Weekdays are meal pods; Fridays are still for the pub.
image_prompt: A stack of sealed meal pods on an office desk, and a busy pub table with pies on a Friday night.
bio: Weekdays are meal pods; Fridays are still for the pub.
summary: A British man eats delivered meal pods during the week for efficiency and meets friends at the pub on Fridays, feeling weekday food has become fuel while weekends keep its social side.

story_text: In 2050 our building in Aarhus runs a zero-waste kitchen club. Leftovers from every flat go into a shared kitchen where volunteers turn them into soups, pickles and bread for the next day. Today I helped make carrot top pesto and a big pot of vegetable soup. It sounds strict, but it feels like a game, and food bills are much lower. I think my generation learned to be creative because we had to.
title: Zero-Waste Kitchen Club
swipe_hook: Our building throws away nothing, not even the carrot tops.
image_prompt: Volunteers in a shared kitchen filling jars with pickles and pesto, crates of leftovers on the floor.
bio: Our building throws away nothing, not even the carrot tops.
summary: A Danish woman volunteers in her building's zero-waste kitchen club, turning residents' leftovers into soups, pickles and bread, which lowers food bills.

story_text: In my day in 2050 fish is expensive because the oceans are protected for most of the year. I eat mostly beans, rice and vegetables, and sometimes cultivated fish that tastes fine but not the same. At Christmas my whole family still buys one real piece of bacalhau and cooks it the old way with potatoes and olive oil. It is the most expensive meal of the year. I understand why things changed, but I feel something was lost.
title: Bacalhau Became a Luxury
swipe_hook: Cod is so rare now that Christmas bacalhau feels like a treasure.
image_prompt: A family table at Christmas with one dish of salt cod, potatoes and olive oil at the centre.
bio: Cod is so rare now that Christmas bacalhau feels like a treasure.
summary: A Portuguese man eats mostly beans, rice and cultivated fish because real fish is rare, but his family still buys one real piece of bacalhau each Christmas. He accepts the change but feels a loss.

story_text: In 2050 I study in Bologna and share a kitchen with five students from different countries. Every evening someone cooks for everyone, so I eat Albanian, Mexican, Korean and Italian food in the same week. Tonight I made byrek with spinach and cheese, and my Korean flatmate added kimchi on the side. It is chaotic and the kitchen is always dirty, but these dinners are the best part of my day.
title: Student Kitchen, Many Flags
swipe_hook: Six students, six countries, one very crowded stove.
image_prompt: Six students around a small kitchen table full of different dishes, steam rising from a pie.
bio: Six students, six countries, one very crowded stove.
summary: An Albanian student in Bologna shares a kitchen with five international flatmates who take turns cooking for everyone, mixing dishes from many countries.

story_text: In 2050 the city recommends insect protein for every meal and gives discounts if you follow the plan. I tried it, and the insect burgers are fine, but on Sundays I make a tortilla de patatas with real eggs from a small farm near Madrid, even though they cost more. My friends come over and we eat it warm with bread. I do not want an algorithm to decide every part of my food.
title: Tortilla Against the Algorithm
swipe_hook: The app says insects; I say my mother's tortilla.
image_prompt: A thick potato omelette on a plate, friends reaching for slices around a small table.
bio: The app says insects; I say my mother's tortilla.
summary: A Spanish woman resists the city's insect-protein meal plan on Sundays by making her mother's potato tortilla with farm eggs for friends.

story_text: In 2050 I work in a building that has a vertical farm in the basement. Every morning I pick up fruit and greens grown downstairs: strawberries, lettuce, herbs. Breakfast is yoghurt with fruit at my desk, and lunch is a salad from the same farm. It is not very romantic, but it is fresh and there is almost no transport. In the evening I cook simple pasta at home and call my parents while I eat.
title: Vertical Farm Breakfast
swipe_hook: Strawberries in January, grown three floors below my office.
image_prompt: Rows of strawberries and lettuce under purple lights in an office basement.
bio: Strawberries in January, grown three floors below my office.
summary: A Frenchman eats fruit and salads grown in his office's basement vertical farm and cooks simple pasta at home in the evening while calling his parents.

story_text: In 2050 almost everything in my kitchen is automated, but in December I bake Christmas cookies by hand from my grandmother's recipes. The flour is from a regional mill and the butter is plant based now, but the tin is the same old blue tin. My brother and I spend a whole weekend baking and arguing about the right shape. The robot cleans up afterwards, which is the only help we accept.
title: Christmas Cookies, Same Tin
swipe_hook: Every December I bake from the same tin my grandmother used.
image_prompt: An old blue biscuit tin full of star-shaped cookies on a floury table, two siblings laughing.
bio: Every December I bake from the same tin my grandmother used.
summary: A German woman and her brother bake Christmas cookies by hand from their grandmother's recipes each December, letting the kitchen robot only clean up.

story_text: In 2050 I live in Dublin in a very small flat, like most young people. The kitchen is one induction plate and a tiny fridge. Most days I eat ready meals or noodles. But once a month I fold pierogi with potato and cheese like my grandmother in Kraków, on a table the size of a laptop. I freeze them and eat them for weeks. Housing changed how we cook more than technology did.
title: Pierogi in a Small Flat
swipe_hook: I fold pierogi on a table the size of a laptop.
image_prompt: A tiny studio kitchen, a young man folding dumplings on a very small table.
bio: I fold pierogi on a table the size of a laptop.
summary: A Polish man in a tiny Dublin flat eats mostly ready meals but makes and freezes his grandmother's pierogi once a month. He feels housing shaped his cooking more than technology.

story_text: In 2050 I live in Leeds and cook something different every evening. I order spices from a cooperative that works directly with farmers in India and Morocco, and I grow coriander and chilies on my windowsill. Tonight I made a chickpea curry with rice and fresh flatbread. Cooking is my break from work. I think food in 2050 is more connected than ever, even if some ingredients are harder to get.
title: Spices From Four Continents
swipe_hook: I order spices from four continents and grow the coriander myself.
image_prompt: A windowsill with pots of coriander and chili, a pan of chickpea curry and flatbread below.
bio: I order spices from four continents and grow the coriander myself.
summary: A woman in Leeds cooks varied dishes each evening with spices from a farmer cooperative and herbs from her windowsill, seeing food as more connected despite scarcer ingredients.

story_text: In my day in 2050 the fridge tracks everything and orders groceries automatically from a local shop. It plans dinners for my family of four based on what we have, so we waste almost nothing. Tonight it suggested fish cakes with potatoes and salad. It is convenient and my kids eat better than I did. Still, sometimes I miss walking through a supermarket and buying something just because it looked good.
title: Smart Fridge Knows Best
swipe_hook: My fridge orders the groceries before I notice they are missing.
image_prompt: A family of four eating fish cakes and salad, a fridge screen glowing in the background.
bio: My fridge orders the groceries before I notice they are missing.
summary: A Danish father lets his smart fridge order groceries and plan family dinners, which cuts waste and improves his children's diet, though he misses spontaneous shopping.
